g12-biology-ub5-t1.overview: The nervous system is the body's wiring: 86 billion neurons exchanging electrochemical signals at meter-per-second to hundred-meter-per-second speeds, organized into the central system (brain and spinal cord — integration) and the peripheral system (nerves — wiring), split functionally into somatic (voluntary muscle) and autonomic (invisceral: sympathetic fight-flight vs parasympathetic rest-digest). This topic runs the signal from receptor to effector — the action potential, the synapse, the reflex — and maps the brain's command layers.
objectives: Describe the neuron's structure and the types (sensory, motor, interneuron)
Explain the resting potential and the action potential mechanism
Trace impulse conduction and saltatory myelin speed-up
Detail synaptic transmission (Ca²⁺ → vesicles → receptors)
Map CNS/PNS organization and the autonomic arms
g12-biology-ub5-t1.simple: A nerve impulse is a wave of chemistry riding electricity. At rest the neuron holds −70 mV (inside negative) by pumping 3 Na⁺ out for 2 K⁺ in and leaking K⁺ back. Stimulus opens Na⁺ channels past threshold (−55 mV) → an all-or-nothing avalanche: Na⁺ floods in (depolarization to +30), Na⁺ gates snap shut and K⁺ channels open (repolarization), a brief undershoot, then the pump restores. The wave cannot go backwards (refractory gates) and does not fade (regenerated at every membrane patch). Myelin insulates and the impulse JUMPS node to node (saltatory: 120 m/s vs 0.5 m/s unmyelinated). At the axon terminal, electricity becomes chemistry: Ca²⁺ enters, vesicles fuse, neurotransmitter crosses the 20-nm cleft, docks on receptors — excite or inhibit the next cell, or a muscle. Reflex arc: receptor → sensory neuron → spinal interneuron → motor neuron → effector, integrated in the cord BEFORE the brain knows you touched the coal.
g12-biology-ub5-t1.detailed:
The cell. Soma (metabolic hub, Nissl bodies = rough ER making proteins and neurotransmitter enzymes), dendrites (the antenna forest — most synapses land here), axon hillock (the decision point: summated potentials are converted to spikes if threshold is reached), axon (myelin sheath from Schwann cells in PNS, oligodendrocytes in CNS; nodes of Ranvier carry the voltage-gated channels), terminals (hundreds of vesicle-loaded buttons). Glia — ten times more numerous than neurons — are not filler: astrocytes build the blood-brain barrier and recycle transmitters, microglia are the resident immune macrophages (Unit 2 again), oligodendrocytes myelinate, and ependymal cells move CSF. Types by job: sensory (afferent, from receptors), motor (efferent, to muscle/gland), interneurons (the CNS's 99%, the processors).

The spike, mechanism by mechanism. Resting potential ≈ −70 mV from the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase (electrogenic 3:2) plus K⁺ leak channels (the membrane is 50-100× more permeable to K⁺ at rest — the Goldman picture). Depolarization past threshold → voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open (positive feedback: the rising phase — a self-amplifying avalanche) → Na⁺ channels inactivate while delayed K⁺ channels open (falling phase) → transient hyperpolarization → reset. Absolute refractory period (Na⁺ gates inactivated: no second spike possible — this FORCES one-way propagation and caps firing rate ~1000/s); relative refractory (stronger stimulus needed — the code for intensity is frequency, not amplitude: spikes are all-or-none letters, rate is the volume dial). Conduction: local currents re-open neighboring channels (continuous in unmyelinated axons); myelin multiplies membrane resistance and the nodes regenerate the spike — faster AND metabolically cheaper (fewer ions to pump back). Multiple sclerosis: the immune system strips CNS myelin — conduction fails in patches, producing the relapsing visual, motor and sensory symptoms: a disease of insulation, not of neurons themselves.

The synapse. Action potential arrives → voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open → Ca²⁺ triggers vesicle fusion (SNARE machinery — the same exocytosis logic as secretion anywhere) → ~10³ transmitter molecules released into the cleft per vesicle → bind postsynaptic receptors: ionotropic (fast: nicotinic ACh channel opens Na⁺ — EPSPs at the neuromuscular junction; GABA-A and glutamate AMPA in the brain) or metabotropic (slow: G-protein cascades, dopamine and most modulatory signals). Termination by reuptake transporters (the serotonin and dopamine transporters — the targets of SSRIs and cocaine), enzymatic degradation (acetylcholinesterase — the target of nerve agents AND of some Alzheimer drugs), or diffusion. Summation: thousands of EPSPs and IPSPs per neuron converge spatially and temporally onto the axon hillock — the cell is a live differential equation deciding, every millisecond, whether to fire. Key transmitters with their fates: ACh (muscle, memory; myasthenia gravis = autoantibodies against its muscle receptor — weakness because the synapse itself is attacked), dopamine (movement and reward; its substantia nigra loss = Parkinson's tremor-rigidity; excess signaling = psychosis), serotonin (mood, sleep, gut; migraine and SSRI logic), GABA (the chief brake; benzodiazepines and alcohol amplify it — the sedative axis), glutamate (the chief accelerator; excitotoxicity kills neurons in stroke when reuptake fails). Drug dependence, in one line: every addiction hijacks the reward dopamine pathway's learning signal.

The system map. CNS: brain + cord, protected by skull/vertebrae, meninges (dura-arachnia-pia), CSF cushion and the blood-brain barrier (tight capillary endothelium — protects but also blocks most drugs: the neuro-pharmacology headache). Brain layers: brainstem (medulla: breathing, heart rate, swallow, vomit; pons: relay and sleep; midbrain: vision/hearing reflexes, dopamine factory) → cerebellum (coordination, timing, motor learning: the drunk-walk is cerebellar suppression by alcohol) → diencephalon (thalamus: the sensory switchboard; hypothalamus: the homeostat — hunger, thirst, temperature, circadian, and the pituitary's commander for t3) → limbic (hippocampus: memory filing — its patient H.M. proved the anatomy; amygdala: fear learning) → cerebrum (four lobes: occipital vision, temporal hearing/language/memory, parietal body sense and space, frontal motor plan + prefrontal judgment — the last to mature at ~25 and the first to fail when tired). Spinal cord: ascending sensory tracts, descending motor tracts (corticospinal), and the segmental reflex machinery; cord transection = the arc below still works (spinal reflexes) but is cut from brain command. PNS: 31 spinal + 12 cranial nerve pairs (the vagus X wanders to the viscera carrying parasympathetic command). Autonomic: sympathetic (thoracolumbar, noradrenaline at targets, the mass fight-or-flight mobilization: heart up, pupils wide, gut closed) vs parasympathetic (craniosacral, ACh, rest-and-digest: the tug-of-war that sets heart rate, gut motility and pupil size). The enteric nervous system — the gut's own 100-million-neuron 'second brain' — rounds the picture.

formulas.name: Frequency code
formulas.meaning: how a constant-magnitude spike encodes a graded world

formulas.name: Summation
formulas.formula: Σ EPSPs + Σ IPSPs vs threshold at hillock

workedExamples.problem: Touch a hot injera mitad: hand jerks before you feel it. Why?
workedExamples.calculation: Reflex arc: 3-5 neurons, cord-level, <50 ms; brain awareness needs ascending tracts + cortex, +100-200 ms.
workedExamples.answer: The cord is the fast local manager; the brain is informed after the fix.

workedExamples.problem: Local anesthetics (lidocaine at the dentist) block pain. Molecular target?
workedExamples.answer: No spike propagation in the numb region's nerves: conduction itself is the victim.

workedExamples.problem: Why doesn't a strong pinch hurt FOREVER?
workedExamples.calculation: Receptors adapt (some fast: touch; slow: pain); refractory caps frequency; descending modulatory circuits damp.
workedExamples.answer: Adaptation and central gating: your nervous system edits continuous inputs.

workedExamples.problem: Tetanus toxin blocks inhibitory interneuron vesicle fusion. Symptom?
workedExamples.calculation: No GABA/glycine braking → motor neurons fire unchecked.
workedExamples.answer: Spastic rigidity (lockjaw): the poison's signature is removing inhibition, matching the mechanism.

commonMistakes: 'The impulse travels as electricity along the whole neuron' (it's an ion-current wave regenerated along membrane; only within a cell, and synapses cross chemically)
Bigger stimulus = bigger action potential (all-or-none: bigger = more frequent)
Myelin 'feeds' the axon (it insulates and speeds; nutrition is Schwann support secondary)
Reflex needs the brain (the arc is spinal; the brain just learns about it)
Sympathetic = bad, parasympathetic = good (they are a coordinated pair; both keep you alive)
applications: Local anesthetics and nerve agents: pharmacology written on the synapse
MS and myelin disease; the kettle-spine of spinal injury rehab
Psychiatric drugs as synapse-engineering (SSRIs, antipsychotics, L-DOPA)
Reflex testing (knee-jerk) as the cord's bedside health probe
g12-biology-ub5-t1.summary: Neurons talk in all-or-none spikes (Na⁺ in, K⁺ out, pump restores), jump them along myelin, translate them at synapses into transmitters, and organize as CNS wiring plus a visceral autonomic tug-of-war — and Ethiopia's own stroke and epilepsy clinics manage the daily consequences.

questions.q: The resting membrane potential is mainly set by:
questions.explanation: K⁺ permeability dominates at rest.

questions.q: An action potential is 'all-or-none' meaning:
options: amplitude is constant once threshold is reached
questions.explanation: Intensity lives in frequency, not size.

questions.q: Myelinated axons conduct faster because:
questions.explanation: Saltatory conduction at Ranvier nodes.

questions.q: At a chemical synapse, Ca²⁺ entry triggers:
questions.explanation: Calcium is the secretion key.

questions.q: Acetylcholinesterase failure (organophosphates) causes:
questions.explanation: ACh accumulates: the synapse can't reset.

questions.q: A withdrawal reflex is integrated in the:
questions.explanation: The arc is local; awareness comes later.

questions.q: Fight-or-flight is which autonomic arm?
questions.explanation: Thoracolumbar, noradrenaline at targets.

questions.q: Parkinson's tremor results from loss of:
options: dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra
questions.explanation: The basal-ganglia dopamine deficit: L-DOPA treats it.

g12-biology-ub5-t2.overview: Sense organs are biological transducers: each converts one physical or chemical energy form into the nerve code every sense shares (frequency-coded action potentials). The eye focuses light onto retinal photoreceptors (rods for night, cones for color), the ear transduces sound waves and head position with hair cells, the nose and tongue read molecules, and skin carries touch, temperature, and pain. This topic runs each instrument — physics in, perception out.
objectives: Explain the eye's optics and retinal transduction
Describe photoreceptor pigments and color vision
Trace the ear's sound path and balance organs
Classify chemoreceptors (taste, smell) and skin receptors
Link common defects (myopia, cataract, deafness) to structures
g12-biology-ub5-t2.simple: Five doors, one hallway. Eye: cornea + lens focus an inverted image on the retina; rods (rhodopsin, night, no color) and cones (three types: S/M/L — red/green/blue mixing gives color) hyperpolarize when light converts their retinal (11-cis→all-trans) and pass signals via bipolar→ganglion cells whose axons form the optic nerve; the blind spot is the nerve's exit; the fovea is the cone-dense acuity peak. Defects: myopia (eyeball too long: near-sight), hypermetropia (far-sight), astigmatism (uneven cornea), presbyopia (aging lens stiffens), cataract (lens clouds), color blindness (missing cone class, X-linked: males ~8%). Ear: pinna→canal→eardrum→ossicles (malleus-incus-stapes: the impedance transformer)→oval window→cochlea; the basilar membrane's position map sorts frequencies (base = high); hair cells bend → nerve. Vestibule + semicircular canals: head position and rotation (the reason spinning makes you dizzy). Nose: ~400 receptor types, combinatorial odor coding, directly wired to limbic (the Proust memory effect). Tongue: sweet, salty, sour, bitter, umami all detectable everywhere (the 'tongue map' is a myth); smell supplies most 'flavor'. Skin: separate receptor organs for touch (Meissner/Pacinian), cold, heat and free-nerve pain.
g12-biology-ub5-t2.detailed:
Eye optics. The cornea does ~2/3 of the focusing power (air→cornea refractive jump), the lens finishes it and fine-tunes by accommodation (ciliary muscle relaxes → zonules taut → lens flat for distance; muscle contracts → lens rounds for near — and the lens stiffens with age: presbyopia, the reading-glasses at 45). Image lands inverted on the retina (inverted by optics, corrected by the brain's calibration — the classic inverted-goggles experiment). Retina inside-out: light passes ganglion layers to reach photoreceptors; the pigment epithelium behind absorbs stray light and recycles retinal (its failure = macular degeneration). Transduction twist: DARK = depolarized rods continuously releasing glutamate (the 'dark current': Na⁺ channels held open by cGMP); LIGHT activates rhodopsin → transducin → phosphodiesterase destroys cGMP → channels close → hyperpolarization → RELEASE DROPS: the signal is a subtraction. Regeneration needs vitamin A (the retinal half — night blindness's earliest sign in deficient children; the Ethiopian context: vitamin-A programs and the orange-fleshed initiatives). Color: trichromatic cone classes (S ~420, M ~530, L ~560 nm) then opponent processing in ganglion cells (red-vs-green, blue-vs-yellow channels: why you can't see 'reddish-green', and why afterimages work). Visual path: optic nerves partially cross at the chiasm (nasal fibers swap: each hemisphere sees the CONTRALATERAL visual field) → LGN → V1 occipital cortex — and the cortex builds perception (the face areas, motion area V5; damage causes agnosias: blindness to meaning, not light).

Ear, the dual instrument. Outer/middle: canal resonance ~3 kHz, ossicles' lever + area-difference transform air vibration into fluid pressure ~20× (why sound barely enters the cochlea directly — the middle ear is an impedance matcher; its muscles damp loud sounds — the acoustic reflex). Inner: cochlea's fluid waves displace the basilar membrane; the traveling-wave place code (base high pitch, apex low: the tonotopic map preserved all the way to cortex); outer hair cells amplify and sharpen (the cochlear 'amp' — its failure = hidden hearing loss; its byproduct: otoacoustic emissions used to screen newborns); inner hair cells do the synapsing. Endolymph's high K⁺ (stria vascularis maintains it: the unusual potassium-driven transduction — bending stereocilia opens tip-link channels, K⁺ enters, depolarizes). Balance: semicircular canals (three orthogonal loops: angular acceleration — cupula drifts; the post-spin nystagmus you can watch in a mirror) and otolith organs (utricle/saccule: gravity and linear acceleration — the head's level; the otoconia dislodged = BPPV's positional vertigo). Deafness taxonomy: conductive (outer/middle: wax, otitis media — the Ethiopian childhood burden of untreated ear infection; tympanic membrane perforation; treatable) vs sensorineural (cochlear/nerve: noise, drugs like aminoglycosides — the TB-treatment era's hidden cost, aging); cochlear implants replace hair cells with electrode arrays at the nerve — the most successful neural prosthesis in medicine.

Chemical senses. Taste: five receptor families on taste cells (ion channels for salty/sour; GPCR cascades for sweet/bitter/umami — bitter alone has ~25 receptor genes: evolution's poison alarm); regenerated every ~10 days; glossopharyngeal + facial to the nucleus solitarius. Smell: olfactory receptor neurons (GPCRs, ~400 functional genes — the largest family) unique in directly REGENERATING from basal cells and in projecting (via the cribriable plate) straight to the olfactory bulb, then limbic/Temporal — no thalamic relay first: the scent-memory-emotion superhighway (why kola and berbere smells flood memory; and why smell loss (post-viral, post-COVID anosmia) degrades FLAVOR so severely — the tongue's five letters vs smell's thousands of words). Flavor = taste + smell + texture (the pinched-nose jellybean test — do it in class). Somatosensory: mechanoreceptor taxonomy (Meissner: light touch/flutter; Pacinian: vibration; Merkel: pressure/texture; Ruffini: stretch), muscle spindles (length — the stretch reflex t1 uses), free nerves (pain, temperature — polymodal; pain's gating theory: rubbing a bumped elbow works because touch fibers compete with pain at the cord — the physiology behind TENS units and the midwife's counter-pressure on a laboring back). Pain's other half is central: descending modulatory pathways (periaqueductal gray → raphe → dorsal horn; enkephalins and opioids close the gate — the placebo analgesia's proven circuitry).

keyTerms.def: touch/descending control at the dorsal horn

formulas.name: Lens equation
formulas.meaning: accommodation varies f to keep focus on the retina

workedExamples.problem: A student sits far, squints, headaches; glasses fix it. Which lens?
workedExamples.calculation: Myopia: image focuses before the retina.
workedExamples.answer: Diverging (concave) lens pushes focus back onto the retina.

workedExamples.problem: Why do you see stars on a dark football field then the ball vanish when looked at directly?
workedExamples.calculation: Rods peak OFF-fovea (parafoveal concentration); fovea is cones-only.
workedExamples.answer: Averted vision uses the rod rich-pan; the central cone zone is blind in the dark.

workedExamples.problem: An aminoglycoside course for TB leaves high-tone deafness. Structure hit?
workedExamples.calculation: Sensorineural: outer hair cells die at the basal (high-frequency) turn first.
workedExamples.answer: The cochlea's bottom: the audiogram's 4 kHz notch is ototoxicity's signature.

workedExamples.problem: Pinch your nose, eat onion vs apple. Same?
workedExamples.calculation: Taste alone: both sweet-sour-mushy; the difference is volatile smell.
workedExamples.answer: Flavor is mostly olfaction: the pinched-nose test proves it.

commonMistakes: Blind spot = where rods are (it's the optic-disc exit — no photoreceptors at all)
Cones work in dim light (rods do: the scotopic/photopic flip)
Sound is 'heard' at the eardrum (transduction is the cochlea)
The tongue map (tastes are not region-partitioned)
Dizziness 'from the eyes' (the vestibular apparatus; vision just corroborates)
Deafness = one disease (conductive vs sensorineural differ in site and treatment)
applications: School vision screening and Ethiopia's eyeglasses programs
Newborn hearing screening via otoacoustic emissions
Cochlear implants: the engineering rescue of sensorineural loss
Aminoglycoside monitoring during TB therapy (ototoxicity surveillance)
g12-biology-ub5-t2.summary: Sense organs turn energy into one common code: optics and retinal subtraction for sight, a fluid place-map for sound and gravity, receptor families for molecules and touch — and each defect tells you which structure fell.

questions.q: Most of the eye's focusing power comes from the:
questions.explanation: The air-cornea jump does ~2/3.

questions.q: Rods differ from cones: rods are for:
questions.explanation: High sensitivity, no color, off-foveal.

questions.q: Light hitting a rod causes it to:
questions.explanation: The dark-current reversal: signals by subtraction.

questions.q: Pitch is encoded mainly by:
questions.explanation: Tonotopy: base high, apex low.

questions.q: The ossicles' essential job is:
options: matching air vibration to fluid pressure
questions.explanation: The impedance transformer of the middle ear.

questions.q: Balance during rotation is sensed by the:
questions.explanation: Cupula drift in three orthogonal loops.

questions.q: Rubbing a bumped elbow reduces pain via:
options: touch fibers gating pain at the cord
questions.explanation: Gate control: competing inputs close the pain relay.

questions.q: Color blindness is usually:
questions.explanation: Mostly M/L pigment gene loss: rarer in females.

g12-biology-ub5-t3.overview: The endocrine system is the body's slow broadcast network: glands secrete hormones — chemical messengers carried by blood to distant targets — that set the pace of growth, metabolism, reproduction, and the minute-to-minute chemistry of blood. This topic maps the glands, the three hormone chemistries (peptides, steroids, amines) and their receptor logics, the hypothalamus-pituitary command chain, and the feedback architectures that make glucose and thyroid control the textbook cases of physiological regulation.
objectives: List major endocrine glands and their chief hormones
Contrast peptide vs steroid hormone mechanisms
Explain hypothalamic-pituitary control (tropics and release)
Describe insulin/glucagon glucose regulation in detail
Diagnose classic disorders from hormone logic (diabetes, goitre, Cushing)
g12-biology-ub5-t3.simple: Hormones: letters the blood delivers. Three chemistries: peptide/protein (insulin, ADH, GH — water-soluble, dock on SURFACE receptors, second messengers relay inside: fast, short-lived), steroid (cortisol, sex hormones — fat-soluble from cholesterol, cross the membrane, dock inside the cell and switch genes directly: slow, long-lived), amine (thyroxine — steroid-like gene action; adrenaline — peptide-like speed). Command chain: hypothalamus reads the body's state and drives the pituitary — its 'master gland' then broadcasts tropic orders (TSH→thyroid, ACTH→adrenal cortex, FSH/LH→gonads) or carries its posterior hormones (ADH, oxytocin — made in the hypothalamus, stored in the back lobe). Each axis ends in negative feedback: too much final hormone silences the upstream signals. The showcase: insulin (fed state: glucose INTO cells, glycogen/fat storage) vs glucagon (fasting: glycogen breakdown, glucose out) — the seesaw that, broken, makes diabetes, the country's fastest-growing endocrine disease.
g12-biology-ub5-t3.detailed:
The gland roster. Hypothalamus (the brain-endocrine interface: releasing/inhibiting hormones to the anterior pituitary via a portal blood system; ADH and oxytocin synthesized here, axon-dumped into the posterior). Pituitary (anterior: GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, prolactin; the target-organ axes below). Thyroid (T3/T4 from iodine + tyrosine: the metabolic thermostat — rate of O₂ consumption, heat, growth permissiveness; calcitonin's minor Ca role). Parathyroids (PTH: the real calcium regulator — bone release, kidney retention, gut activation via vitamin D). Adrenals (cortex zones: mineralocorticoids/aldosterone-salt, glucocorticoids/cortisol-stress and metabolism, androgens; medulla: adrenaline — the sympathetic's hormonal echo, fight-flight amplified and prolonged). Pancreas's islets (β insulin, α glucagon — the blood-sugar governor). Gonads (testosterone, estrogen/progesterone: pubertal build, gamete environments, cycle). Plus the diffuse organs now recognized as endocrine: gut hormones, kidney erythropoietin (the altitude answer — EPO's renal factory), heart natriuretic peptide, adipose leptin (the satiety signal — Unit 3's budget hormone), and thymus (the immune-education organ that shrinks after childhood: the thymus-and-immunity line Unit 2 needed).

Mechanism: two delivery logics. Peptide hormones (all water-soluble): can't enter cells → bind membrane receptors → G-protein/second-messenger cascades (cAMP for adrenaline and glucagon — Sutherland's discovery, why ONE adrenaline molecule becomes a MILLION glucose releases: amplification) or kinase-linked (insulin's receptor is itself a tyrosine kinase — autophosphorylation cascades moving GLUT4 glucose transporters to muscle and fat: exercise does the same job through a different door — the physiology behind 'movement lowers blood sugar'). Steroid hormones: lipophilic, diffuse in, bind intracellular/nuclear receptor-transcription-factor complexes → gene expression changes → proteins made over hours-days: cortisol's anti-inflammatory reprogramming, testosterone's muscle build, estrogen's cycle architecture. Because steroids act genomically they are slow and long — and because their receptors are transcription factors, small hormone changes move big protein programs. Thyroid hormone breaks the pattern: an amine that acts like a steroid (nuclear receptors, metabolic gene program). The clinical mirror: antibodies against receptors — Graves' (TSH receptor stuck ON: hyperthyroid) and the receptor-blocking type of insulin resistance: receptor diseases read the mechanism directly.

Two full cases. GLUCOSE: after a teff-based breakfast, glucose rises → β cells release insulin → liver/muscle/fat take up glucose, store as glycogen/fat, blood falls → falling glucose signals → α cells release glucagon → liver glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis (Unit 3's pathway in service) → glucose restored. Type 1: autoimmune β destruction → no insulin → cells starve amid plenty, fat burned wildly (ketones), blood sugar toxic; needs injected insulin; often pediatric-onset. Type 2: receptors resist insulin (visceral fat, inactivity, genetics) → β cells overwork then fail → adult-typical but rising in Ethiopian towns with diet shift; treated by metformin, weight, movement, sometimes insulin. The HbA1c test: glucose permanently glycating hemoglobin — a three-month average written in protein: endocrine diagnostics as chemistry forensics. THYROID THERMOSTAT: cold/need → hypothalamus TRH → pituitary TSH → thyroid T3/T4 → tissues burn faster, heat rises → T3/T4 feed back on pituitary and hypothalamus (negative feedback: the level stat reads itself). Iodine shortage → no T3/T4 → feedback silence → TSH floods → thyroid hypertrophies: GOITRE — the simple goitre belt of the highlands (soils leached, dairy-grain diets low in iodine) and why universal salt iodization (USI) — Ethiopia's 1990s-onward program — is endocrinology as public health. Hashimoto's (autoimmune hypothyroid: fatigue, cold, weight) vs Graves' (autoimmune hyper: heat, tremor, bulging eyes): the same gland, two immune errors, opposite metabolisms.

Stress and salt. The stress axis: hypothalamus CRH → pituitary ACTH → adrenal cortex cortisol — mobilize glucose, spare immune alertness in the short run; chronic stress/cortisol: belly fat, suppressed immunity (the psychoneuroimmunology bridge back to Unit 2), memory-hippocampus damage, and Cushing's syndrome (excess: moon face, thin skin) vs Addison's (gland failure: bronze skin, low pressure — TB's historic destruction of the adrenals, Ethiopia's own textbook cause). Aldosterone (the mineralocorticoid lane): low blood pressure/salt → renin-angiotensin cascade → aldosterone → kidney saves Na⁺ (water follows) → pressure restored: the RAAS the whole antihypertensive drug industry targets (ACE inhibitors — the 'prils'). ADH (posterior): osmoreceptors detect thick blood → water reabsorption in kidney collecting ducts; failure (diabetes insipidus: ADH-less, liters of dilute urine — NOT the sugar disease despite the shared name) shows the naming trap. Oxytocin: uterine contraction and milk ejection (the baby's suckle → maternal reflex: positive feedback — the rare loop that amplifies until delivery ends it). Growth hormone: childhood excess = gigantism, deficit = dwarfism; adult excess = acromegaly (the brow and hands grow). Melatonin: the pineal's night signal, the circadian clock's voice (the sleep-wake axis Unit 5's behavioral pages lean on).

formulas.name: Feedback loop
formulas.formula: Hypo → Releasing hormone → Pituitary tropic → Gland hormone → (⊖ back up)

workedExamples.problem: A patient: high blood glucose, high insulin, still diabetic. Type?
workedExamples.calculation: Type 2 = receptor resistance: the gland answers, targets ignore.
workedExamples.answer: Peripheral resistance: insulin high, action low — the obesity-linked lane.

workedExamples.problem: Graves' disease: TSH is LOW yet thyroid overworks. Why?
workedExamples.calculation: Antibodies stimulate the receptor directly; T3/T4 high → pituitary suppressed.
workedExamples.answer: Read the axis backwards: low tropic + high product = the gland is driven from ELSEWHERE.

workedExamples.problem: Addison's: low cortisol, HIGH ACTH, bronze skin. Mechanism?
workedExamples.calculation: Gland failure → no feedback → ACTH floods; ACTH's peptide shares melanocyte-stimulating sequence.
workedExamples.answer: The pigmentation is the scream of the pituitary: diagnosis printed on skin.

workedExamples.problem: Why does a highland village show more goitre than a coastal one?
workedExamples.calculation: Leached volcanic soils + no sea-food iodine; the axis starves for raw material.
workedExamples.answer: Geography writes endocrinology: iodization fixed what the soil lacked.

commonMistakes: 'Pituitary is the boss' (the hypothalamus runs the board; the pituitary is the broadcaster)
Confusing diabetes mellitus (insulin) with insipidus (ADH) — shared name, different disease
Steroids 'enter and act immediately' (genomic action: hours to days)
Insulin raises blood sugar (it LOWERS it — glucagon raises)
Goitre = always too little iodine (also excess-drive conditions and autoimmune)
Hormones 'destroy' things (they only change rates of existing machinery)
applications: Universal salt iodization: endocrine disease prevented at the factory
Metformin, insulin and the diabetes epidemic's urban shift
Cortisol's immune brake: prednisone prescribed, Addison's missed
EPO physiology: altitude, anemia and the blood-doping abuse
g12-biology-ub5-t3.summary: Glands broadcast three hormone chemistries through blood; the hypothalamus-pituitary axes run every downstream gland on negative feedback, and the two showcase loops — insulin/glucagon and TRH/TSH/T4 — explain diabetes and goitre from mechanism to public health.

questions.q: Steroid hormones act mainly by:
options: binding intracellular receptors to change gene expression
questions.explanation: Lipophilic: the genomic route, slow and lasting.

questions.q: TSH is made by the:
questions.explanation: The tropic order to the thyroid.

questions.q: After a meal, blood glucose falls because:
questions.explanation: The fed-state storage command.

questions.q: Iodine deficiency causes goitre because:
options: thyroid lacks raw material so TSH floods and the gland enlarges
questions.explanation: Feedback silence drives pituitary output.

questions.q: ADH acts on the kidney to:
questions.explanation: The water-balance gate.

questions.q: Cortisol's chronic excess does ALL EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: It SUPPRESSES immune function — Cushing's logic.

questions.q: Type 1 diabetes' cause is:
questions.explanation: No insulin made: injection needed.

questions.q: The hypothalamus controls the anterior pituitary by:
options: releasing hormones in a portal blood link
questions.explanation: A vascular chat: the portal system.

g12-biology-ub5-t4.overview: Homeostasis is the body's standing project: keeping internal chemistry — temperature, water, salt, glucose, pH, calcium, blood pressure — within narrow bands while the outside world swings. Every control system in this book (nervous, endocrine, kidney, skin, liver, lungs) is a piece of homeostatic machinery, and the general architecture is the same everywhere: receptor, control center, effector, negative feedback. This topic unifies Unit 5 and previews Unit 6's stress on those systems.
objectives: Define homeostasis, set point, and dynamic equilibrium
Name the control-loop parts in any physiological example
Explain thermoregulation in hot and cold detail
Describe osmoregulation and kidney control (ADH loop)
Generalize feedback to disease (diabetes, fever, hypertension)
g12-biology-ub5-t4.simple: A thermostat in every basement. Every loop: a sensor detects error from a set point, an integrator (usually brain) compares, an effector corrects, and the correction FEEDS BACK to shut the loop off — negative feedback, the body's steering wheel (it turns against the drift). Examples: temperature (hypothalamus 37 °C; skin and core thermoreceptors; effectors = sweat, vessels, shivering, behavior); water (osmoreceptors → ADH → kidney; thirst as the behavioral arm); glucose (β/α cells and liver — t3's seesaw); blood pressure (baroreceptors → autonomic → heart/vessels; RAAS the slow lane); pH (lungs blow off CO₂ fast, kidneys rebuild bicarbonate slow); calcium (PTH vs calcitonin on bone, kidney, gut). Homeostasis is NOT constancy — it is dynamic equilibrium: the line on the recorder wobbles around a set point, and 'health' is the loop's gain and range. Fever RESETS the set point upward (pyrogens re-program the hypothalamus: the chills are the body obeying the new order). Disease, in this language, is a broken loop: sensor, center, effector, or feedback.
g12-biology-ub5-t4.detailed:
The architecture. A control system = receptor (error detector), comparator/integrator (reference value), effector (the correcting muscle/gland), feedback path (the correction returns to the sensor — negative: opposes the disturbance; the rare positive: amplifies to an endpoint — childbirth's oxytocin, the blood-clotting cascade). Set points themselves are adjusted by circadian rhythm (afternoon peak, dawn trough — the reason medicines are timed), age, and pathology (the fever reset). Claude Bernard's 'milieu intérieur' — the internal sea kept separate from the external one — and Cannon's coining of 'homeostasis' with the fight-or-flight follow-up (Selye's general adaptation syndrome: alarm → resistance → exhaustion: the cost of holding a loop against sustained load: the cortisol story of t3's stress axis from the system level).

Thermoregulation, full loop. Inputs: cold/warm receptors in skin + hypothalamic temperature-sensing cells. Effector menu: hot — cutaneous vasodilation (radiate: the flushed runner), sweating (evaporation's 2.4 kJ per gram — the highland dry-air sweat evaporates before you notice: the injera-baker's invisible water loss and why the cool dry climate is a thermal advantage the lowlands lack), behavior (shade, water, light clothing); cold — vasoconstriction (the core-save: cold hands to keep the heart warm), piloerection (goosebumps: our vestigial fur-raise), shivering (motor centers drumbling muscles — heat without work), non-shivering thermogenesis (brown-fat uncouplers: Unit 3's gradient leak on demand), and behavior — the jacket, the fire, the huddle. Fever: pyrogens (IL-1, TNF from macrophages — the immune system's voice joining the hypothalamus; prostaglandin E₂ is the final mediator — the reason aspirin/paracetamol cut fever: they block it) reset the set point up; the rising phase is COLD physiology (chills, gooseflesh) obeying the new target; the break is HOT physiology (sweat, flush). The heat ceiling: proteins denature past ~42 °C; the cold floor: below ~28 °C the heart's rhythm fails — hypothermia's slow window. Ethiopia's field reality: highland day-nights that swing 20 °C — the schoolchild's morning-fire and midday-sleeve-removal is behavioral thermoregulation as daily practice.

Osmoregulation and the pressure loops. Water: hypothalamic osmoreceptors (cell shrinkage = concentration) drive thirst AND posterior ADH release; kidney collecting-duct water channels (aquaporin-2) open only with ADH: without it, dilute urine floods out (the water-drinker's suppression), with it, urine concentrates several-fold (the dry-season herder's conservation — Borana cattle and people both run on renal concentrating power). The salt-pressure slow lane: juxtaglomerular cells sense pressure → renin → angiotensin II (a vasoconstrictor AND aldosterone releaser AND thirst-stimulator — one molecule, three effectors: a whole loop's worth) → salt-water retention + pressure restored: the RAAS; the baroreflex fast lane: carotid/aortic pressure receptors → medulla → vagal/sympathetic balance adjusted beat-to-beat (the orthostatic dizziness on standing fast: the loop's lag, then it catches up — why the elderly, with stiffer sensors, fall). pH: CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ — the lungs set the CO₂ term by minutes (hyperventilation at altitude: the respiratory compensation for thin air that tips pH alkaline; the kidney then dumps bicarbonate to re-level: acclimatization's quiet chemistry), the kidneys set the bicarbonate term by days. Calcium: PTH raises blood Ca²⁺ (bone osteoclasts, kidney retention, kidney's vitamin-D activation → gut absorption); calcitonin is the weak brake; the loop's breakdown shows in tetany (low Ca: nerves fire spontaneously — the hand claws) and bones' quiet dissolving in hyperparathyroidism.

Integration and the Unit 6 bridge. One system's proof: every loop of this topic shares parts — the hypothalamus is the master integrator (temperature, osmolarity, hunger via leptin/insulin signals, stress, circadian), the medulla the autonomic switchboard, the kidneys the chemical plant, the skin the radiator, the liver the glucose bank, the lungs the pH throttle. Disease as loop failure, named: diabetes mellitus (signal failure: t3), diabetes insipidus (ADH absence), essential hypertension (sensor gain loss and RAAS overdrive), heat stroke (evaporation capacity exceeded — the loop saturated), altitude sickness (hypoxia; HIF biology driving EPO acclimatization over weeks), and dialysis as homeostasis outsourced to a machine. And the stressor Unit 6 makes central: when ambient temperature and water scarcity exceed the loop's range — climate change is, biologically, an assault on homeostasis' operating envelope, one whose victims are the people whose bodies still do the hauling, herding and farming the loops evolved for.

keyTerms.def: the reference value a loop defends

formulas.name: Control loop
formulas.formula: error = set point − sensor value → response opposes error

formulas.name: Bicarbonate buffer
formulas.meaning: pH held by lung (CO₂) and kidney (HCO₃⁻) on opposite sides

workedExamples.problem: Standing up fast from a squat: vision greys for a second, then clears. Trace the loop.
workedExamples.calculation: Pressure fell (blood pooled in legs) → baroreceptor firing dropped → medulla lifted sympathetic tone → vessels constricted, heart sped.
workedExamples.answer: The clearing IS the homeostasis: you watched a reflex run.

workedExamples.problem: Why the chills at the START of a fever, before it shows on the thermometer?
workedExamples.calculation: Pyrogen raised the set point; current 37 is now 'cold' → shiver + vasoconstrict until blood hits the new target.
workedExamples.answer: Chills are the obeying of a changed order: the loop works fine — its reference moved.

workedExamples.problem: A Borana herder on a long dry trek makes small, dark, strong-smelling urine. Which loop?
workedExamples.calculation: Hyperosmotic blood → ADH maximum → aquaporin-2 open → water reclaimed.
workedExamples.answer: Concentrating ability at its ceiling: the kidney's daily gift to the drought.

workedExamples.problem: Newly arrived at 3 000 m: breathe fast all night; headaches fade in days. Chemistry?
workedExamples.calculation: Hyperventilation blows CO₂ → respiratory alkalosis → kidney excretes bicarbonate → pH normalizes and breathing can settle.
workedExamples.answer: Acclimatization = two loops cooperating: lungs act fast, kidneys re-level over days.

commonMistakes: Homeostasis = fixed values (it is dynamic range: the wobble is the design)
Sweating cools by the water's temperature (it is EVAPORATION's latent heat)
Fever 'is the illness' (it is a re-set regulation with a defense side: heat slows many pathogens and speeds immune kinetics — Unit 3's Q₁₀ again)
Positive feedback = always bad (clotting and birth use it to finish jobs)
ADH makes dilute urine (it makes CONCENTRATED urine: saves water)
The kidney only 'cleans' (it is a homeostatic organ: salt, water, pressure, pH, red-cell signals)
applications: Heat-wave and midday-labor guidance: loop-saturation prevention
Oral rehydration salts: exploiting gut Na-glucose co-transport (Unit 3 chemistry saving Unit 5 physiology)
ACE inhibitors and diuretics: pharmacology pointed at the pressure loop
g12-biology-ub5-t4.summary: Homeostasis is negative feedback everywhere: sensors compare state to set points and effectors correct (temperature, water, salt, sugar, pH, calcium), and nearly every disease in this unit is the same story — a loop broken, reset, or saturated.

questions.q: Homeostasis is best defined as:
options: dynamic maintenance of internal ranges via feedback
questions.explanation: A defended wobble, not a frozen line.

questions.q: Sweating cools the body mainly by:
questions.explanation: 2.4 kJ leaves with each gram evaporated.

questions.q: The chills at fever onset mean:
options: set point raised; effectors obey the new target
questions.explanation: Reference moved; correction began.

questions.q: ADH's target is the kidney's:
questions.explanation: Aquaporin-2 insertion: water reclaimed.

questions.q: Blood pH is regulated by which pair?
questions.explanation: CO₂ fast side, bicarbonate slow side.

questions.q: Shivering generates heat by:
questions.explanation: Motor drumbling: heat without locomotion.

questions.q: A positive-feedback example is:
questions.explanation: Amplify to the delivery endpoint, then stop.

questions.q: Quick-standing dizziness that clears shows:
options: the baroreflex catching up after pressure lag
questions.explanation: Transient lag, then correction: the loop working.
